paragraphs: A great distinction must be made between parties. Some countries are so large that the different populations living in them have conflicting interests, even though they are subjects of the same government, and they may therefore be in a perpetual state of opposition. In that case the different sections of the people are better regarded as distinct nations than as mere parties. If a civil war breaks out, the struggle is carried on by rival peoples rather than by factions within a single state.

But when citizens hold different opinions on subjects that affect the whole country equally, such as the principles on which the government should be conducted, then divisions arise that may rightly be called parties. Parties are a necessary evil in free governments, but they do not always have the same character and the same tendencies.

At certain times a nation may be oppressed by such unbearable evils that it plans to change its political constitution completely. At other times the trouble lies deeper still, and the very existence of society is in danger. These are the times of great revolutions and great parties. But between these epochs of misery and confusion there are periods when human society seems to be at rest and mankind seems to pause. This pause is only apparent, for time does not stop for nations any more than for men. They are all advancing toward a goal they do not know, and we imagine them stationary only when their progress escapes our notice, just as men walking at a slow pace seem to be standing still to those who are running.

But whatever the truth of this, there are certain epochs when the changes in the social and political constitution of nations are so slow and so imperceptible that men imagine their present condition to be final. The human mind, believing itself firmly based on certain foundations, does not extend its inquiries beyond the horizon it can see. These are the times of small parties and of intrigue.

The political parties I call great are those that cling to principles more than to their consequences, to general cases and not to particular ones, to ideas and not to men. These parties are usually marked by a nobler character, more generous passions, more genuine convictions, and bolder and more open conduct than the others. In them private interest, which always plays the chief part in political passions, is more carefully veiled under the pretext of the public good. It may even sometimes be hidden from the very people whom it excites and drives.

Minor parties, on the other hand, generally lack political faith. Because no lofty purpose sustains or dignifies them, they openly show the selfishness of their character in their actions. They glow with an artificial zeal. Their language is violent, but their conduct is timid and irresolute. The means they use are as wretched as the end they aim at. That is why, when a calm period follows a violent revolution, the leaders of society seem suddenly to vanish and the powers of the human mind seem to lie hidden. Great parties convulse society; minor ones merely agitate it. The former tear it apart, the latter degrade it. And if the great parties sometimes save it by a healthy shock, the minor ones always disturb it to no good purpose.

America has already lost the great parties that once divided the nation. Her happiness has increased considerably, but her morality has suffered from their disappearance. When the War of Independence was over and the foundations of the new government had to be laid, the nation was divided between two opinions. These two opinions are as old as the world, and they are met with perpetually, under all the forms and names that have ever existed in free communities. One tended to limit the power of the people, the other to extend it indefinitely. The conflict between them never reached in America the degree of violence it has often shown elsewhere. Both American parties were in fact agreed on the most essential points. Neither had to destroy a traditional constitution or overthrow the structure of society in order to secure its own triumph. Consequently, in neither of them were many private interests affected by success or defeat. But moral principles of a high order, such as the love of equality and of independence, were at stake in the struggle, and they were enough to kindle violent passions.

The party that wished to limit the power of the people tried to apply its doctrines especially to the Constitution of the Union, and from this it took its name of Federal. The other party, which claimed to be more exclusively attached to the cause of liberty, took the name of Republican. America is a land of democracy, and the Federalists were always in a minority. But they counted on their side almost all the great men whom the War of Independence had brought forward, and their moral influence was very considerable. Circumstances also favored their cause. The collapse of the Confederation had given the people a dread of anarchy, and the Federalists did not fail to profit from this passing mood of the multitude. For ten or twelve years they were at the head of affairs, and they were able to apply some, though not all, of their principles, for the opposing current was growing too violent day by day to be checked or resisted. In 1801 the Republicans took control of the government. Thomas Jefferson was elected President, and he increased the influence of their party by the weight of his fame, the greatness of his talents, and the immense extent of his popularity.

The means by which the Federalists had held their position were artificial, and their resources were temporary. They had risen to power through the virtues or the talents of their leaders. When the Republicans reached that high station, their opponents were crushed by a complete defeat. An immense majority declared itself against the outgoing party, and the Federalists found themselves in so small a minority that they at once despaired of future success. From that moment the Republican or Democratic party *a has gone from conquest to conquest, until it has gained absolute supremacy in the country. The Federalists saw that they were beaten beyond recovery and isolated in the midst of the nation. They split into two groups. One joined the victorious Republicans; the other abandoned its rallying point and its name. Many years have now passed since they ceased to exist as a party.

a [ [It is scarcely necessary to remark that in more recent times the meaning of these terms has changed. The Republicans are the representatives of the old Federalists, and the Democrats of the old Republicans.—Trans. Note (1861).]] In my opinion, the rise of the Federalists to power was one of the most fortunate events that accompanied the formation of the great American Union. They resisted the inevitable tendencies of their age and country. But whether their theories were good or bad, they had the defect of being unworkable, as a system, in the society they claimed to govern, and what happened under Jefferson must therefore have happened sooner or later. Still, their government gave the new republic time to gain a certain stability, and afterward to withstand the rapid growth of the very doctrines they had fought against. A considerable number of their principles were in fact built into the political creed of their opponents, and the Federal Constitution that exists today is a lasting monument to their patriotism and their wisdom.

Great political parties, then, are not found in the United States at the present time. There are parties that threaten the future tranquillity of the Union, but none that seem to contest the present form of government or the present course of society. The parties that endanger the Union rest not on abstract principles but on material interests. These interests, scattered across the provinces of so vast an empire, may be said to form rival nations rather than parties. Thus, on a recent occasion, the North argued for a system of commercial prohibition and the South took up arms in favor of free trade, simply because the North is a manufacturing region and the South an agricultural one, and the restrictive system that benefited the one was harmful to the other. *b

b [ [The divisions between North and South have since become far more intense, and the South, though conquered, still shows a formidable spirit of opposition to Northern government.—Translator’s Note, 1875.]]

In the absence of great parties, the United States swarms with lesser controversies, and public opinion is divided into a thousand tiny shades of difference over questions of very little importance. The pains taken to create parties are beyond belief, and at present it is no easy task. In the United States there is no religious animosity, because all religion is respected and no sect is dominant. There is no jealousy of rank, because the people is everything and no one can challenge its authority. Lastly, there is no widespread poverty to supply the means of agitation, because the physical position of the country opens so wide a field to industry that a man can accomplish the most surprising undertakings with his own native resources. Nevertheless, ambitious men have an interest in creating parties, since it is hard to remove a person from office merely because others covet his place. The skill of the players in the political world therefore lies in the art of creating parties. A political aspirant in the United States begins by identifying his own interest and calculating which other interests might gather around it and combine with it. Then he manages to find some doctrine or principle that will suit the purposes of this new association, and he adopts it in order to bring his party forward and win popularity. It is like the imprimatur of a king in former days, which was bound into the volume it authorized although it had nothing to do with the book. When these preliminaries are finished, the new party is introduced into the political world.

To a stranger, all the domestic controversies of the Americans seem at first so incomprehensible and so childish that he does not know whether to pity a people that takes such arrant trifles seriously or to envy the happiness that lets it discuss them. But when he studies the secret tendencies that govern the factions of America, he easily sees that most of them are more or less connected with one or the other of those two divisions that have always existed in free communities. The deeper we look into the workings of these parties, the more we see that the aim of the one is to limit, and that of the other to extend, the authority of the people. I do not claim that the declared aim, or even the secret aim, of American parties is to promote the rule of aristocracy or of democracy in the country. But I do affirm that aristocratic or democratic passions can easily be found at the bottom of all parties, and that, although they escape superficial observation, they are the main point and the very soul of every faction in the United States.

To take a recent example: when the President attacked the Bank, the country was stirred up and parties were formed. The well-informed classes rallied to the Bank, the common people to the President. But it must not be imagined that the people had formed a reasoned opinion on a question that presents so many difficulties even to the most experienced statesmen. The Bank is a great institution with an independent existence, and the people, accustomed to making and unmaking whatever it pleases, is startled to meet this obstacle to its authority. In the midst of the constant change in society, the community is irritated by so permanent an institution and is led to attack it, to see whether it can be shaken and controlled like all the other institutions of the country.
Remains of the Aristocratic Party in the United States

Secret opposition of wealthy individuals to democracy — Their retirement — Their taste for exclusive pleasures and for luxury at home — Their simplicity in public — Their affected condescension toward the people.

It sometimes happens that, among a people with a variety of opinions, the balance between the several parties is lost, and one of them gains an irresistible preponderance. It overcomes every obstacle, harasses its opponents, and takes all the resources of society for its own purposes. The defeated citizens despair of success, and they hide their dissatisfaction in silence and general apathy. The nation seems to be governed by a single principle, and the dominant party claims the credit for having restored peace and unanimity to the country. But this apparent unanimity is merely a cloak for alarming dissension and perpetual opposition.

This is exactly what happened in America. When the democratic party gained the upper hand, it took exclusive possession of the conduct of affairs, and from that time the laws and the customs of society have been shaped to suit its whims. Today the wealthier classes are so completely removed from the direction of political affairs in the United States that wealth, far from giving a right to exercise power, is more of an obstacle than a means of reaching it. The wealthy members of the community leave the arena, unwilling to contend, and often to contend in vain, against the poorest of their fellow citizens. They concentrate all their enjoyments in the privacy of their homes, where they hold a rank they cannot assume in public, and they form a private society within the state, with its own tastes and its own pleasures. They submit to this state of things as an incurable evil, but they are careful not to show that it galls them. It is even not uncommon to hear them in public praising the delights of republican government and the advantages of democratic institutions. Next to hating their enemies, men are most inclined to flatter them.

Look, for instance, at that wealthy citizen, who is as anxious to conceal his wealth as a Jew of the Middle Ages. His dress is plain, his manner unassuming. But the inside of his house glitters with luxury, and only a few chosen guests, whom he haughtily calls his equals, are allowed into this sanctuary. No European noble is more exclusive in his pleasures, or more jealous of the smallest advantages his privileged position gives him. Yet the very same man crosses the city to reach a dark counting-house in the center of trade, where anyone who likes may approach him. If he meets his cobbler on the way, they stop and talk. The two citizens discuss the affairs of the state, in which they have an equal interest, and they shake hands before they part.

But beneath this artificial enthusiasm and these servile attentions to the dominant power, it is easy to see that the wealthy members of the community have a hearty distaste for the democratic institutions of their country. The populace is at once the object of their scorn and of their fears. If the mismanagement of the democracy ever brings on a revolutionary crisis, and if monarchical institutions ever become practicable in the United States, the truth of what I am saying will become obvious.
The two chief weapons that parties use to ensure success are the public press and the formation of associations.
